aspects.title: CSS visual-vs-DOM reorder: judging whether the source-order read still preserves meaning (F1 FAIL vs Example-2 PASS)
aspects.description: A page uses CSS (absolute/relative positioning, flexbox order, flex-direction:row-reverse, grid-area/grid-template-areas) so the visual order differs from DOM source order. A tool can mechanically detect 'visual order != DOM order', but that mismatch is ONLY a 1.3.2 failure when reading the content in source order changes the MEANING. The SC pairs the explicit non-failure (Example 2: nav / main / side-story CSS-reordered, meaning unaffected = PASS) directly against the failure (F1 Products/Locations two-column example, where source order reads 'Products Locations Telephones Computers Portable MP3 Players Wisconsin Idaho' and Wisconsin/Idaho bind to the wrong column = FAIL). Note the F1 trap: source order has item5 (Wisconsin) BEFORE item4 (Idaho), so values are swapped even within one logical column — purely semantic, invisible to a DOM-diff tool. The evaluator must linearize the content, read it as prose, and decide whether it still parses as the intended meaning. This is the central, most-tested discrimination of the SC.
aspects.scLimb: Core requirement: 'When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined' — applied to CSS-positioned content (F1, C27, G57).
aspects.whyUncovered: The SC 1.3.2 inventory reports actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0 — there is literally zero ACT coverage of any facet of this SC. Even a hypothetical tool that flagged every visual!=DOM mismatch would fire on the Example-2 PASS case (nav reorder, meaning unaffected) as a false positive, and could not read the linearized text to confirm the F1 FAIL case actually scrambles meaning. Distinguishing FAIL from PASS is a semantic reading task, not a markup or DOM-diff check, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse cannot reliably do it.

references.quote: The order of content in a sequence is not always meaningful. For example, the relative order of the main section of a web page and a navigation section does not affect their meaning. They could occur in either order in the programmatically determined reading sequence.
Providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning.

Determine whether the reading order of content is still understandable after linearization.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pairs of near-identical-looking layouts: one where CSS reorder breaks meaning (FAIL) and one where the same visual layout keeps meaning intact in source order (PASS), to force the semantic discrimination rather than a blind 'any reorder = fail' rule. Use position:absolute, flex order, flex-direction:row-reverse, and grid-area as the reordering mechanisms. Always include at least one PASS page where CSS reorder is harmless (Example-2 style) so the annotator is penalized for over-flagging. Keep each page self-contained with inline <style>.
suggestedScenarios: Two-column pricing comparison: left column DOM lists 'Plan A, Plan B'; a separate CSS-positioned price column whose DOM order is reversed, so linearized it reads 'Plan A Plan B $19 $9' and prices bind to the wrong plan (FAIL), versus an identical-looking layout where DOM keeps each plan adjacent to its price (PASS).
Recipe using flex-direction:row-reverse so steps render 1,2,3 visually but DOM order is 3,2,1; linearized the instructions are dangerously out of sequence (add eggs before mixing the batter).

A confirmation dialog whose 'Cancel / OK' buttons are CSS-reordered so source order reads 'OK Cancel' while visual is 'Cancel OK', reversing the affordance order spoken to AT (arguable FAIL), beside a page where a nav bar is absolutely positioned to the top but appears LAST in the DOM with meaning unaffected (Example-2 PASS).
A CSS grid scoreboard where grid-area positions 'Home 3 — Away 1' visually but DOM order interleaves to read 'Home Away 3 1', detaching each score from its team.
A before/after medical-advice card visually ordered Before-then-After, but DOM has After first; linearized, the warning 'do not eat beforehand' reads as the outcome rather than the precaution.

A pure layout-reflow page where CSS order moves a decorative pull-quote ahead of the article body in source order but it reads fine either way (PASS) — a deliberate trap to test the annotator does NOT over-flag every CSS reorder.

aspects.title: Layout-table linearization that scrambles a meaningful sequence (F49) — reading 2-D content as a linear story
aspects.description: An HTML <table> used purely for layout (WCAG explicitly permits layout tables) presents content that reads correctly in two visual dimensions, but when linearized row-by-row, cell-by-cell, the meaningful sequence breaks. F49's two canonical cases: (1) the advertisement where a rowspan stitches 'XYZ mountaineering top!' into one line and separates it from 'XYZ gets you to the', destroying the slogan 'XYZ gets you to the top!'; (2) the museum page where left-column nav links are interleaved with the right-column image/placard/heading/description, so the description is shredded by Link 2, Link 3, Link 4... The evaluator must mentally linearize the cell reading order (first cell of first row to last cell of last row, reading nested cells fully) and judge whether the resulting prose still tells the same story — a semantic reading task over a 2-D structure.
aspects.scLimb: Layout-table-linearization failure mode (F49) + G57 'placement of blocks of content using layout tables may produce a rendering in which related information is positioned together visually, but separated in the content stream.'
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F49 is a failure technique only. Critically, axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do NOT flag layout tables as 1.3.2 failures — a layout table is valid HTML and WCAG permits it — so there is no automated signal. The failure lies entirely in whether the linearized cell order preserves meaning, which requires reading the cells in linearization order and reasoning about the story, something no automated checker does.

aspects.title: Faked columns / faked tables in pre-formatted plain text (F33, F34): visual 2-D structure with zero DOM structure

Visually it looks like two columns or a grid; in the linear character stream a screen reader reads ACROSS the fake columns, interleaving them into gibberish (e.g. 'Web Content Accessibility Guidelines including blindness and low vision'). There is NO table/column markup at all — so the only signal is that the rendered visual implies a 2-D structure the linear character stream destroys. The evaluator must look at the rendering, recognize the implied columnar/tabular structure, then read the character stream and judge that the linear reading scrambles the meaning.
aspects.scLimb: White-space-multi-column-plain-text (F33) and white-space-table-in-plain-text (F34) failure modes (the 1.3.2 facet of these shared 1.3.1/1.3.2 failures).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; F33/F34 are failure techniques only. Automated checkers have nothing structural to assert against — there is no <table>, no CSS columns, just a blob of text in <pre>/<textarea>. axe/WAVE see only text and cannot tell the whitespace encodes a visual grid whose linearization is nonsense. Recognizing the faked 2-D structure from the rendering and judging that the character stream scrambles meaning is inherently visual + semantic.

aspects.title: Responsive-breakpoint source-vs-visual desync — order is meaningful at one viewport but reordered at another
aspects.description: A single self-contained page is correct in DOM source order at one width, but a media query reorders flex/grid items at another breakpoint such that the visual order no longer matches the meaningful source order — e.g. a 'Step 1 / Step 2 / Step 3' wizard whose mobile media query uses 'order:' to stack the steps 2,1,3; or an 'Editor's note: read the conclusion first' sidebar that on mobile collapses ABOVE the content it refers to, turning a closing note into a misleading lede. The failure exists only in one rendering state, so the evaluator must render at multiple viewports, recognize that the order is meaningful, and confirm that the visual order diverges from the meaningful source order at the breakpoint where meaning is order-dependent. (Distinct from the F1 single-viewport case: the failure is conditional on viewport and requires comparing rendered states.)
aspects.scLimb: Core requirement applied to CSS flow-order reflow across responsive breakpoints (C27 'each order may be meaningful in itself but may cause confusion'; implied by F1/C27 but named by no failure technique).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2, and no failure technique names responsive 'order:' reflow specifically. Automated DOM-vs-visual diff tools typically run at a single viewport and have no notion that a breakpoint reorder changes meaning; they cannot judge whether the reordered sequence still parses, nor will they think to compare across breakpoints.

aspects.title: Bidirectional / mixed-directionality text where the visual order is fixed by reordering characters, exposing the wrong order to AT (G57 bidi case)
aspects.description: A page mixes LTR and RTL scripts (English + Arabic/Hebrew/Persian, or numbers/punctuation embedded in RTL text). G57 names the precise failure: an author 'fixes' the visual rendering by physically moving characters in the content stream (e.g. relocating a trailing period or a price) so the Unicode bidi algorithm happens to position them correctly on screen — but this exposes the WRONG logical character order to AT. The correct fix is markup (dir, <bdi>, <bdo>) that overrides the bidi algorithm so the order is right both visually AND to AT, NOT reordering source characters. Conversely, omitting needed dir/bdi markup can leave the visual correct but the logical order scrambled when spoken. Detecting this requires reading both scripts, knowing their directionality, and judging whether the logical (source) order matches the visual.
aspects.scLimb: Bidirectional / RTL text-order limb (G57: 'using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm' rather than reordering source characters).
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2; G57 is a general technique with no ACT rule/test. The failure is invisible to automated structural checkers: the markup may be well-formed and the visual rendering correct; only by reading both scripts and comparing logical-vs-visual order can one tell that source characters were reordered (exposing wrong order to AT) or that bidi markup was wrongly omitted. This requires multilingual semantic judgement no checker performs.

references.quote: The visual rendering problem could be corrected by moving the punctuation in the content stream so that the bidirectional algorithm positions it as desired, but this would expose the incorrect content order to assistive technology.
The content is both rendered in the correct order visually and exposed to assistive technology in the correct order by using markup to override the bidirectional algorithm.

It is important that it be possible to programmatically determine at least
         one sequence of the content that makes sense.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Construct short mixed-direction strings (English + Arabic/Hebrew, or RTL text with embedded LTR numbers/punctuation/prices). Create the FAIL version by physically reordering characters in the source to force a correct-looking visual via the bidi algorithm (or by omitting needed dir/bdi), and a PASS version that achieves the same visual using dir/<bdi>/<bdo> markup with logical source order intact. Include a side-by-side so the annotator compares logical vs visual order. Keep strings short and self-contained.
suggestedScenarios: An Arabic sentence ending with a price '$50.' where the source has the digits/period physically reordered to render correctly via bidi (FAIL: spoken order wrong), beside a version using <bdi> with logical source order (PASS).
A Hebrew label followed by an English product code, where omitting dir causes the visual to look right but the logical/spoken order interleaves the code into the label.
An English UI string containing an embedded Arabic name where a trailing comma was moved in the source to fix the visual, exposing the wrong order to AT.
A Persian paragraph with an embedded LTR URL where source-character reordering yields a correct visual but a scrambled programmatic reading order.
A bilingual breadcrumb mixing RTL section names and LTR page names where missing dir markup makes the separator '>' bind to the wrong segment when read.
A correctly-marked-up mixed-direction sentence using dir and <bdo> that is right both visually and logically (PASS) — a trap to ensure not every RTL+LTR mix is flagged.

aspects.title: Applicability gate and multiple-valid-orders: deciding whether order is meaningful at all, and that more than one order can be correct
aspects.description: 1.3.2 only applies 'when the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning,' and the Understanding adds three clarifications: providing a particular linear order is only required where it affects meaning; there may be more than one 'correct' order; only one correct order needs to be provided. Two independent non-interleaved articles, a nav-vs-main pairing, and a magazine article with callout sidebars can each appear in EITHER order without failing — the container has no meaningful sequence even though each article does. The evaluator must first decide whether order is meaningful for the content at hand (the applicability gate), and must NOT flag a page merely because its block order could be different, as long as no single block's internal meaning is broken. This is the discrimination that prevents over-flagging the whole SC.
aspects.scLimb: Conditional applicability trigger ('When the sequence... affects its meaning') + multiple-valid-orders limb ('There may be more than one order that is correct... Only one correct order needs to be provided').
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT coverage for 1.3.2. Nothing in ACT tests the applicability gate — deciding whether order is meaningful at all — and no rule/test/technique exercises the multiple-valid-orders case. EN 301 549 frames C.9.1.3.2 as Inspection with a 'Not applicable... does not contain content relevant' clause, wholly absent from ACT. A checker cannot decide whether reordering two articles or a nav/main pair affects meaning; that is a contextual semantic judgement, and getting it wrong means false positives on perfectly conformant pages.

There may be more than one order that is "correct" (according to the WCAG 2 definition).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages whose block-level order COULD be different but where each block's internal meaning is intact (PASS, not applicable / multiple valid orders), interleaved with pages where reordering DOES break meaning (FAIL). The point is to test whether the annotator correctly applies the applicability gate and does not flag conformant pages. Mix order-irrelevant containers (independent articles, nav/main, sidebars) with genuinely order-dependent content (steps, instructions). Self-contained pages.
suggestedScenarios: A page with two fully independent, non-interleaved articles whose source order differs from a 'natural' reading guess but neither article's internal meaning is affected (PASS — container has no meaningful sequence).

A magazine-style article with two callout sidebars placed in source order before the main body; the order of article-vs-sidebars does not affect meaning (PASS), beside a page where a sidebar is interleaved INTO the middle of a sentence (FAIL).
A landing page where the nav section appears after the main content in the DOM (Example-2 style); order does not affect meaning (PASS).
A dashboard of independent widgets (weather, stocks, calendar) in an arbitrary order where any permutation reads sensibly (PASS — multiple correct orders).
A numbered step-by-step assembly guide whose blocks are in scrambled source order so the steps read out of sequence (FAIL — order IS meaningful), to contrast with the order-irrelevant PASS cases.

A news homepage with several unrelated story teasers in one order, plus a second copy in a different order, both of which read fine (PASS — only one correct order needs to be provided), to test the annotator does not flag order-flexible containers.

pages.scenario: SaaS two-plan pricing comparison built from position:absolute chips. Plans authored low-to-high (Starter, Growth); the two price chips emitted in REVERSE source order ($79 first, then $19). CSS coordinates land each price in the correct visual column, but linearized the page reads 'Starter ... Growth ... $79 ... $19', binding the expensive price to the cheaper plan and swapping the prices relative to source.
pages.mechanism: position:absolute on every .plan and .price; the .price chips' DOM order is the reverse of the .plan cards' DOM order (F1 archetype), so the programmatically-determined reading sequence binds each price to the wrong plan.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All elements have visible text; nothing is empty, unlabeled, or low-contrast, so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse find nothing. No checker models which price belongs to which plan, so it cannot detect the reversed price column; even a hypothetical visual!=DOM diff tool could see the mismatch but could not read the linearized stream and judge that the prices bind to the wrong plans.

citation.quote: This describes the failure condition that results when CSS, rather than structural markup, is used to modify the visual layout of the content, and the modified layout changes the meaning of the content.

pages.scenario: Recipe blog 'Brown-Butter Madeleines' with a four-step Method as a real <ol>. flex-direction:row-reverse + flex-wrap:wrap-reverse renders the cards 1,2,3,4 top-to-bottom while the <ol> source order is 4,3,2,1. Because an ordered list is an inherently meaningful sequence, a screen reader announces 'item 1 of 4' on the BAKE step, linearizing the recipe into a dangerous order (bake the batter before mixing it).
pages.mechanism: display:flex with flex-direction:row-reverse and flex-wrap:wrap-reverse on ol.steps inverts the rendered order vs source; the <ol> (a WCAG-defined meaningful sequence) is read 4-3-2-1 by AT, the reverse of the correct cooking order. Hand-typed .n badges mask the reversal visually.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <ol> is valid, every <li> has text, no empty nodes or contrast issues. Tools do not compute that flex-direction:row-reverse inverted the visual order vs source, and even detecting the geometric mismatch would not tell a tool that THESE steps must be performed in order (a recipe) rather than an unordered set. Judging the reversed sequence is dangerous is human comprehension.

citation.quote: The semantics of some elements define whether or not their content is a meaningful sequence. For instance, in HTML, text is always a meaningful sequence. Tables and ordered lists are meaningful sequences, but unordered lists are not.

pages.scenario: News article 'The tidal marsh is coming back' with TWO deliberate CSS reorders: a position:fixed <nav> that is LAST in source order, and a decorative <blockquote> pull-quote placed FIRST in the DOM but grid-rendered in the side rail. A mechanical visual!=DOM detector fires on both, but neither changes meaning (Example-2 PASS / over-flag trap): the nav, article, and pull-quote are independent blocks and the article is self-contained.
pages.mechanism: position:fixed nav (DOM-last) + CSS-grid-placed blockquote (DOM-first) create visual!=DOM mismatches on independent blocks. Linearized order pull-quote -> article -> nav still conveys correct meaning because no block depends on another's position; this is the SC's own Example 2 non-failure.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This is the inverse trap: a naive visual-vs-DOM diff tool raises a FALSE POSITIVE because it detects the mismatch but cannot read the linearized prose to confirm meaning survives. Distinguishing this harmless reorder from a genuine F1 failure requires reading the content and judging block independence, a semantic decision automated tools cannot make.

citation.quote: Example 2: CSS is used to position a navigation bar, the main story on a page, and a side story. The visual presentation of the sections does not match the programmatically determined order, but the meaning of the page does not depend on the order of the sections.

pages.scenario: Football full-time scoreboard rendered as 'Hillside Harriers 3 / Riverton Wanderers 1' via CSS grid-template-areas. The four grid items are authored grouped by type, not by team: both team names first, then both scores (DOM 'Harriers, Wanderers, 3, 1'). grid-area re-pairs each score with its team visually, but linearized the scores detach from their teams.
pages.mechanism: display:grid + grid-template-areas + grid-area placement re-pair items visually while the DOM groups team,team,score,score. The accessibility tree follows source order with no programmatic team-to-score association, so AT speaks 'Harriers, Wanderers, 3, 1' and the result is unrecoverable.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each cell has valid text; no empty nodes, missing names, or contrast failures. Tools do not reconstruct the visual grid pairing from grid-area rules to compare against source order, and detecting the geometric mismatch would not tell a tool that '3' must be read right after 'Hillside Harriers' to convey the score. Binding a number to the adjacent team is content comprehension.

citation.quote: Assistive technologies rely on the source code or other programmatically determined order to render the content in the correct sequence. Thus, it is important not to rely on CSS to visually position content in a specific sequence if this sequence results in a meaning that is different from the programmatically determined reading order.

pages.scenario: Airline booking confirmation itinerary. Each leg visually shows Depart -> Arrive (Outbound 07:15 BUE -> 10:05 SCL; Return 19:40 SCL -> 22:30 BUE) via grid-template-areas. After a two-pass i18n refactor the markup authors ALL departures first, then ALL arrivals, so DOM order is Outbound, Return, 07:15-dep, 19:40-dep, 10:05-arr, 22:30-arr. Linearized, the two departures are read back-to-back then the two arrivals, scrambling which time belongs to which leg.
pages.mechanism: display:grid + grid-template-areas pairs each leg's depart/arrive visually while the DOM is field-grouped (all departures then all arrivals). AT reads the field-grouped source order, detaching each flight's departure from its arrival and binding the return departure (19:40) to the outbound arrival (10:05).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All times and labels are real text; no empty cells, missing names, or contrast problems. A tool cannot know a flight leg's depart and arrive must be read adjacently, nor reconstruct the grid pairing from grid-area to notice the source groups by field. Judging that the linearized stream scrambles the legs requires reading it as an itinerary.

citation.quote: The order in which items appear on a screen may be different than the order they are found in the source document. Assistive technologies rely on the source code or other programmatically determined order to render the content in the correct sequence.

pages.scenario: Museum exhibition page 'Currents'. On wide screens flexbox order renders the Visit info box (hours/admission/location) in the LEFT rail and the essay on the right, while the DOM is content-first (essay first, Visit aside second). A visual!=DOM detector fires (the DOM-second aside renders left of the DOM-first essay), but it is the G57/Example-2 non-failure: the blocks are independent and each is internally well-ordered. Over-flag trap.
pages.mechanism: display:flex with order:2 on article.essay and order:1 on aside.visit swaps their visual position relative to a content-first DOM. The essay and the Visit box are independent meaningful sequences, and within each block source order is correct (hours in day order; paragraphs intro->detail->closing), so linearizing preserves meaning.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A naive visual-vs-DOM diff tool raises a FALSE POSITIVE: it detects flex order swapped the aside and essay but cannot read the linearized prose to confirm meaning survives. Telling this harmless reorder apart from a genuine F1 failure requires reading the content and judging block independence and internal order, which no automated tool can do.

pages.scenario: Mountaineering-retailer promo banner built as a layout table: a wordmark cell and a giant italic 'top!' in a rowspan=2 bottom-aligned cell visually finish the slogan in the row below ('Summit Provisions gets you to the top!'), but the rowspan places 'top!' before the clause in source order. This is F49's canonical advertisement case.
pages.mechanism: A rowspan=2 cell reorders the content stream so the punch word 'top!' is read before the clause it completes; linearized DOM order (verified via Puppeteer) is 'Summit Provisions Mountaineering Outfitters | top! | Summit Provisions gets you to the', splitting the slogan that is a meaningful sequence.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: A layout table is valid HTML and WCAG permits it; role=presentation is the correct marking, every cell has text, contrast passes, no attribute is missing. No checker reads the linearized cell stream and judges that '...top! ...gets you to the' has stopped making sense — that is a human semantic reading task over a 2-D structure.

pages.scenario: A gallery exhibition page (Thornbury Gallery) where a layout table puts a left-hand nav column, a tall rowspanned artwork image, then a placard + 'About this work' heading + five-paragraph description. Visually the description is one coherent column of prose, but the rowspanned image and per-row nav cells interleave nav links between the description paragraphs when linearized. This is F49's museum case 2.
pages.mechanism: The artwork cell is rowspan=8 while nav links sit one-per-row in the leftmost column, so linearized DOM order (verified) interleaves description paragraphs with 'Membership', 'Plan Your Visit', 'Shop the Catalogue', 'Accessibility' links — the single meaningful sequence describing the painting is shredded by intervening links.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every link has text and an href, the image has a text alternative, the heading is a real h2, role=presentation correctly marks the layout table; nothing is missing or malformed so axe/WAVE/Lighthouse report nothing. pages.scenario: A cafe loyalty coupon (Bean & Leaf) laid out as two side-by-side 'stamps' in a 2x2 layout table with a dashed divider. A divider + stacked typography cue the eye to read DOWN each column (left stamp: 'Buy one'/'get one free'; right stamp: '$10 espresso flight'/'with code SAVE25'), but the table is encoded row-major so linearization scrambles the offer.
pages.mechanism: Visual/intended reading is column-major but the four content cells are in row-major DOM order, so linearized order (verified) is 'Buy one | $10 espresso flight | get one free | with code SAVE25' — the BOGO promise 'Buy one ... get one free' is split with the price line wedged between its two halves.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The 2x2 grid is valid HTML, role=presentation is correct, all four cells have visible text, nothing is empty. Automated tools do not reconstruct the intended visual reading order (here column-major, cued by a divider and stacked layout) nor judge that the row-major linearized stream has ceased to be a coherent offer — a human visual + semantic comparison.

pages.scenario: A bilingual parallel-text page presenting Antonio Machado's 'Caminante, son tus huellas' with the Spanish poem in the left column and a facing English translation in the right column, in a layout table. Each column is a self-contained four-line poem; row-major linearization interleaves the two languages line by line and each cell carries a lang switch. Long-tail i18n variant of F49.
pages.mechanism: The two columns are each a complete poem (a meaningful sequence) meant to be read whole, but row-major DOM order (verified) interleaves them: 'Caminante, son tus huellas | Wanderer, your footprints are | el camino y nada más; | the road and nothing more; ...'. Both poems are shattered as sequences, and per-cell lang=es flips the synthesizer voice on every line.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: This page scores WELL on naive checks: every Spanish cell has correct lang=es, every cell has text, role=presentation is set, and there is no header/data relationship to fault. No tool has a concept that the two columns are each a self-contained poem that row-major linearization splices together — that is a human literary/reading judgment.

pages.scenario: A food newsletter (The Saturday Kitchen) built as a bulletproof nested-table HTML email. A dish photo sits in the left column with heading/intro/CTA on the right; the photo's caption was placed in a second outer-table row to baseline-align with the body text, so linearization reads photo -> whole recipe blurb -> caption, divorcing the caption from its image.
pages.mechanism: Because layout tables linearize row-by-row and nested tables are read in full first (F49), the verified DOM order is photo aria-label -> 'Red-wine short ribs / intro / Get the full recipe' -> 'Pictured: short ribs after three hours, glaze reduced by half.' The caption arrives after the entire blurb with no figure/figcaption/aria-describedby tie, so the image->caption sequence is broken (G57's caption-in-following-row warning).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The image has an aria-label, every cell has content, the tables are correctly role=presentation, and the nested-table structure is the industry-standard bulletproof email pattern no linter faults. Tools do not reconstruct that the later caption describes an earlier image nor that the linearized order interposes the whole blurb between them — associating caption with image across linearized cells is a human reading judgment.

citation.quote: Since layout tables are read row by row, if the caption of an illustration is placed in the row following the illustration, it may be impossible to associate the caption with the image.

pages.scenario: Control / PASS trap: a 'How returns work' explainer (SwiftShip) built as a 2-column layout table, one row per numbered step ([number badge | step text]) stacked in order 1, 2, 3. It is a genuine layout table marked role=presentation with no th — exactly like the failing cases — but it linearizes correctly, so an annotator must actually linearize rather than reflex-flag every layout table.

A reviewer must read the cells in source order and judge the procedure still makes sense; flagging it merely for being a layout table would be a false positive.

pages.scenario: Desktop-software EULA install screen renders the license body as a single monospaced <pre> inside a focusable scroll region. To fit the page, two unrelated clauses are laid out as newspaper columns with padding spaces: each source line holds a fragment of the LEFT clause, a space gutter, then a fragment of a DIFFERENT RIGHT clause. Sighted users read each column top-to-bottom; AT reads each line across, splicing the grant clause into the middle of the reverse-engineering/transfer restriction clause.
pages.mechanism: F33 — white-space characters create two columns in plain text. The column relationship exists only as space padding inside one <pre> (no <table>, no CSS column-count). A screen reader reads the character stream in line order, so the first spoken line becomes '1. GRANT OF LICENSE. Aperture Software grants and may not be reverse engineered,' — clause 1's opening fused onto the restriction clause's middle. No correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined, so the legalese the user must accept is unintelligible.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The markup is valid and complete: a labelled role=region, a real <pre>, properly-associated checkbox and Continue button. No rule fires for 'this preformatted text visually forms two columns.' axe/WAVE/Lighthouse operate on the DOM/character stream and have no model of the rendered monospace geometry, so they cannot detect that the visual layout implies a two-column reading order the linear DOM order shatters. pages.scenario: A self-service 'Team Email Signature' tool outputs a ready-to-paste signature in a read-only <textarea>. The signature is a directory card whose rows align three columns — Name | Title | Phone — using literal TAB characters (tab-size:12, monospace). pages.scenario: A user-submitted guitar chord chart for 'Harbor Lights' uses the universal chords-above-lyrics convention: a chord line and a lyric line alternate, and each chord is padded with leading spaces so that, in a monospace font, it sits directly ABOVE the exact syllable where the chord change happens. There is no <ruby>, table, or data attribute — only leading-space alignment encodes which chord goes with which word; a <span class=chord> merely colors the chord text.

A screen reader reads in document order: it speaks the entire chord line as a detached run of chord names ('G C G') and then, separately, the entire lyric line.
